id: spine (macro shape) / world.md 'The ending, as world fact' / E-a E-b
resembles: Final Fantasy X (a pilgrim's sacrifice buys a Calm that lasts years; the cycle broken by refusing the 'proven way' and finding another)
Dark Souls (link the fire to prolong the age vs let it go out)
Hollow Knight (a vessel chosen to contain a burning thing; the ending offers taking its place)
Madoka Magica (a cycle of sacrificed girls broken by redistributing the cost)
Le Guin, 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas', and Jemisin's answer 'The Ones Who Stay and Fight'
why: The whole arc is 'a world kept alive by one sacrificed person; the mentor offers the proven way of renewing the sacrifice for a generation; the hero breaks the cycle by sharing the cost'. That is the stock shape of FFX and of Dark Souls' ending menu, and the E-b/E-a pair is that menu. A genre reader identifies the ending by B44 at the latest. The plan's 'spent turns' sit inside this frame rather than turning it. flat-story.md names upward drift and early resolution as the largest risk for a grim story; E-a is the bright 'power of the town' end the frame predicts.
proposed_turn: Keep the sacrifice-cycle convention but take a left turn on what breaks it: the holder still forgets, and what changes is that the town remembers for them (the chronicle, N9, N8 tell the next 'you' who you are), so the cycle continues but stops destroying the town. Or let the Hearth only partly work, so the real ending is the town carrying a cost the player watches it pay.

id: world.md 'The player's real situation' (amnesiac immortal, ruins of own previous towns, notes in own hand)
resembles: Planescape: Torment (immortal amnesiac who returns from death, finds his own previous incarnations' notes and works, journal in his hand)
Returnal (finds her own earlier selves' logs and corpses in the ruins)
Memento
Dark Souls (the Undead who returns at a bonfire)
why: Every element (wake with no memory, return from death at one spot, notes in your own hand you didn't write, a past self who got further, layers of your own previous attempts) is Planescape: Torment's core, which genre readers treat as the canonical version. The plan's turn ('you were a battery, not hero or villain') is real, but it is also Torment's and Hollow Knight's answer shape (an empty vessel used by others).
proposed_turn: Let the previous selves disagree: old-hand notes that contradict each other (one past you tried to leave, one tried to refuse), so the past is several people rather than one hidden truth. mysteries.md currently says old-ink corrections are 'always right', which is the Torment convention unturned.

id: B40 / world.md 'The yes' (registry line 'will not refuse' turns the running 'you said yes' joke into the twist)
resembles: BioShock ('Would you kindly': a running phrasing revealed as the protagonist's conditioned compliance)
The Stanley Parable (the player's obedience as the joke)
Hollow Knight ('No mind to think. No will to break.': the vessel selected for lacking will)
why: A repeated line about the player always complying, revealed by a document to be a trait they were selected or made for, is BioShock's famous twist; any player who has played it completes B40 the moment the registry is mentioned, and the plan calls this the player's own turn. The game's yes is also mechanically the player's choice, so 'you were selected for it' quietly says the player's choices were the character's conditioning, which BioShock already made its point of.
proposed_turn: Keep the registry and the dry form, but make the selection line about availability, not temperament ('no dependants; nearest'), with the pencil tick still in your hand: the yes stays yours, and the joke turns on being a nobody who volunteered rather than on being built to obey.

id: world.md 'Magic: the rules' (nothing made only moved; like calls like; links; heat moved from a stone)
resembles: Patrick Rothfuss, The Name of the Wind (sympathy: heat drawn from a source, links by like material, slippage; the plan even uses the word 'sympathy' for keel links)
Fullmetal Alchemist (equivalent exchange)
Frazer, The Golden Bough (sympathetic magic, the law of similarity and contagion)
why: Rules 1 and 3, and B15's lesson that warming one thing cools another, are Kingkiller's sympathy nearly beat for beat; a fantasy reader names it. Ash as the tithe (rule 2) and memory as the heaviest coin (rule 5) are what is distinctive. A familiar magic system is acceptable in a game that teaches it; the risk is in the vocabulary and in B15 being the same classroom demonstration.
proposed_turn: Never say 'sympathy' in canon or text; lead with the tithe, the visible grey hands and drifts, so the player meets the cost before the law. Let B15's failure produce ash on the field rather than only a cold stone, so the lesson is the game's own rule 2 rather than Kvothe's.

id: world.md 'What broke, and how' (the Concord drew cheaply from something vast and cooling under the land, then burned it)
resembles: Final Fantasy VII (Shinra draining the living Planet's Lifestream as Mako)
N. K. Jemisin, The Broken Earth (an empire powered by drawing on a living Earth, enslaved orogenes, ash-sky Season)
Dark Souls (the First Flame fading, prolonged by sacrifice)
why: Empire powers itself from a living thing under the world, it sickens, catastrophe follows: FFVII and Broken Earth. Broken Earth also supplies ash skies, a long cold, and human batteries (node maintainers) kept to quell the land, which is the holder. The bureaucratic euphemism ('Deep Account', 'acceptable tithe') is the turn and is good; the extraction premise underneath is stock.
proposed_turn: Lean the cause onto the paperwork rather than the extraction: the Kindling was a budget decision made by clerks to cover a shortfall, recorded as a line item, so the catastrophe reads as accountancy rather than hubris. Keep the cooling-body hint, but cut what duplicates Broken Earth (see the ridges and scream finding).

id: world.md 'Names' and 'Bureaucracy' humor (Concord euphemisms, 'Holder (1), replaceable', clerks filing in a dead city)
resembles: Terry Gilliam, Brazil
Control (the Federal Bureau of Control)
Pratchett's Discworld civil service
why: Bureaucratic euphemism as a world-ender, kept dry, is the plan's freshest register and it fits the Tally theme. It has relatives but nobody files 'accounting-mages whose ledger killed the world' as template. Keep it, and spend more of the turns here (see the B40 and Kindling findings).

id: world.md 'The running motif: the stool'
why: A wobbly stool, short on the same leg in every layer of ruins, never explained, used as joke first and as the 'again' turn later: specific, concrete, small, and not a stock symbol. It does exactly what llm-tells' 'turn' asks (a concrete thing the reader completes). Do not fix it. The one risk is E-b's 'the stool goes in the cellar for next time', which ties a bow on it; let the ending's last image be the stool unchanged rather than placed.

id: B1 / opening-v2 P1-P2 (wake in a ruin under falling ash, alone, nothing in your head; book with torn pages)
resembles: A Dark Room (and its lineage, Candy Box)
Dark Souls III (the Ashen One rising from a grave in ash)
Planescape: Torment (wake in a mortuary with no memory)
The Elder Scrolls (wake a nameless prisoner)
why: Already on writing-craft.md §4's worn list. It is shipped and hard to move. The amnesia is fine as convention; what is worn is announcing it.
proposed_turn: Since it ships, turn the telling, not the beat: never state the memory loss in a log line; let the first thing the player 'knows' be practical and wrong-handed (the boot finding the slab's edge, P4), so the amnesia is inferred from competence the player can't account for.

id: day-one H7 (prints to the larder, three roots gone, a strip of smoked meat left that you didn't smoke)
resembles: A Dark Room ('a stranger approaches the fire')
why: It keeps A Dark Room's stranger convention and takes a left turn: the stranger shows up first as a fair trade by someone unseen, which tells you their character before their face. Concrete, implied, no explanation. Keep.

id: B3 (N1 walks out of the ash, the last of five, sees food to spare and sits down)
resembles: A Dark Room (the stranger at the fire)
Frostpunk / The Walking Dead (the hardened lone survivor who joins)
why: After H7 the arrival itself lands as the stock version. 'The last of five' is a told backstory hook of the kind llm-writing.md lists as exposition. Shipped, so turn small.
proposed_turn: Let her not sit at once: she eats, leaves something of hers by the warm stone, and comes back the next visit; or drop 'the last of five' from anything the player sees and let the cart at B4 imply the others.

id: B4 (fetch her people's cart; it's gone, wolf prints all round; she takes the news without a word)
why: A first quest that fails, outcome no_and, with the grief left in a silence: the first offer ends worse than it started, against the model's upward drift. Good.

id: B7 (wolves at the edge; a fine fight; meanwhile the pack strips the drying racks)
why: A win that is a loss, made of animal behaviour, not a twist. Exactly the 'yes, but' flat-story.md asks for, and concrete. Keep.

id: world.md wrist mark / mysteries Q1 (a scar-like mark on the wrist matching N3's and the holder's mark over the keel door)
resembles: Dark Souls (the Darksign, the brand of the Undead who return from death)
Berserk (the Brand of Sacrifice)
Harry Potter (the scar)
why: A body mark that identifies the chosen or cursed returner and matches a symbol over a door is a stock chosen-one tell, and here it is the Darksign almost exactly (a mark on those who return at a fire). It also makes N3's identity readable at B19 (see N3).
proposed_turn: Make it a Concord clerk's stamp, an inked or seared filing mark that becomes legible once B33 teaches Concord script, so the player reads their own label ('Holder, Hollow, 1 of 1'), turning the brand into paperwork, which is this world's joke.

id: B12 / B36 / opening-v2 P6 (circles round a circle: pressed-through ghost drawing, cellar doodle, layered ruins, the keel ring plan, the finished design at B49)
resembles: Close Encounters of the Third Kind (the compulsive drawing that turns out to be the plan)
Planescape: Torment
why: The repeated diagram, seen as doodle early and as blueprint late, is a stock 'the symbol was the answer' device, and it now appears at P6 (minute 12), B12, B16, B30, B36 and B49: six showings make it a signpost rather than a hindsight clue. mysteries.md's own rule is that clues are mundane and 'ominous only in hindsight'; six repeats of one glyph aren't.
proposed_turn: Cut two showings (B16's table scratching and either P6 or B12), and let the last showing differ from the others: the finished design at B49 is a circle of many small circles, which the earlier half-drawings never were, so the reveal is the change, not the recognition.

id: B16 (a newcomer stares through supper, gone before dawn, circles scratched in the table)
resembles: the stock 'stranger who recognises the amnesiac and flees' (Planescape: Torment, The Bourne Identity)
why: Recognition-and-flight is a common amnesia-thriller beat; with the scratched glyph it also over-signals. B34 (N9) does the same recognition better, so B16 spends it early.
proposed_turn: Keep the stare, drop the glyph: the newcomer leaves their bowl and a set of snares tied your way, so the only clue is a craft habit, which hands B34 and H4's snare thread something to pay.

id: B5 / B27 / B32 (warm ground; 'the heat everyone survives on comes from here'; putting the burn out would freeze everyone)
resembles: Dark Souls (the fire that must not go out)
Frostpunk (the heat source the town lives or dies by)
Snowpiercer (the engine that is the problem and the only life)
why: world.md lists B32 as one of four spent turns ('fix the catastrophe' turns). But the player is taught warm ground as life from minute 3 (opening P3), at B5, B13 and B27 ('the heat everyone survives on comes from here'). By B46 the 'putting it out kills us' reveal is a confirmation the player made weeks earlier, and the beat is told: 'you look for a way to put the burn out, and find it'. flat-story.md: a beat that ends where it started is activity, not an event.
proposed_turn: Make the player cause it: an Arcana or project choice caps a seam to calm a surge (F4 is right there), and an outpost freezes. The goal changes because of a cost the player paid, not because a document says so.

id: B13 (the first Clear: a pale sun, the whole town stops to look)
resembles: Ray Bradbury, 'All Summer in a Day'
Frostpunk / The Road (the rare sun as hope)
why: The town stopping in wonder at the sun is the warm stock image, a soft upbeat moment of the kind llm-tells #10 calls a hopeful closer. It is a clock beat and can stay; it needs one wrong note.
proposed_turn: Something casts a shadow it shouldn't, or the old ones don't look up at all because they remember it lasts a week, so the wonder belongs only to the newcomers.

id: B18 / creatures.md Pilgrim (corpses walked toward warm ground by the fungus in them; spores get into the food)
resembles: The Last of Us (cordyceps-driven dead)
M. R. Carey, The Girl With All the Gifts
Annihilation
Bloodborne / Dark Souls fungal hollows (unsure)
why: Fungus walking the dead is the most worn creature idea of the last decade. 'Pathos, not horror' and 'shows where seams are' is a real turn in function, but the silhouette ('a corpse walking very slowly, mushrooms at the collar') is TLoU's image, and 'spores get into the food' is TLoU's threat.
proposed_turn: Keep the fungus and the heat-seeking, change the host: the fungus walks the dead forest's trees' fallen trunks or a dead elk, not people, and the human version is the town's own burial custom (lay the dead on warm ground so they walk to the seam) which N4 tends. The horror then is a choice the town makes.

id: B19 / cast.md N3 Sorrel (gentle stranger who declines every offer, flinches at 'hold', same wrist mark; is the refuser who broke the world)
resembles: Le Guin, 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas' (the one who walked away)
Memento / Before I Go to Sleep / 50 First Dates (forgets each day; diary 'who wrote this?')
Planescape: Torment (the companion tied to your past)
why: The twist (B42) is good; the clueing gives it away. A stranger who arrives at B19 with your wrist mark, refuses everything in a game about saying yes, and flinches at the word 'hold' at B21 is solved by a genre reader 40 days before B42. world.md's guardrail is 'never stated; laid side by side', but the side-by-side starts on arrival. The daily-forgetting diary is the Memento/Before I Go to Sleep device unturned.
proposed_turn: Drop the flinch and hide the mark (sleeve, or it's the stamp and illegible until B33); let N3 decline only offers that would bind them (stay a night, hold a rope, take a name), accepting others, so the pattern is something the player notices late. Their diary could drop the 'who wrote this?' opener and simply contradict itself.

id: E-c (N3 holds the Hearth; says yes for the first time; forgets daily so offers again every morning)
resembles: 50 First Dates (the daily-repeated consent, inverted)
why: The refuser becoming the one who says yes every morning without remembering is odd, tender and earned by two optional offers. It is the plan's best ending. Keep it, and resist explaining why it costs them little; let the morning offer be the last image.

id: B20 / regions.md Death ('Kept, are you.' The town shrugs at returners)
resembles: Dark Souls (bonfire return, the Undead as a known condition)
Hades (everyone treats Zagreus's returns as routine)
Hollow Knight (benches)
why: Return at a fixed fire after death, with the world shrugging, is Dark Souls' mechanic plus Hades' comedy; both are now the default framing. The shrug is the plan's own turn, and Hades already took it.
proposed_turn: Make the shrug cost something social: the town's attitude to 'the kept' is practical and slightly mercenary (they send you on the dangerous jobs, cast.md's Wall faction already splits on it), so returning becomes a reason you carry the night-soil cart, which is the competence-against-status humor world.md wants.

id: B21 / cast.md N4 / factions (faith-keeper of Old Warmth; the Faithful vs the Ledger; a town held round a heat source in a frozen world)
resembles: Frostpunk ('Faith Keepers' is Frostpunk's own term; its Faith vs Order paths; the Generator town; discontent factions)
Lovecraft ('that is not dead which can eternal lie'; don't wake the sleeper)
why: A town surviving around a heat source in a frozen land, with a faith-keeper and a Faith-versus-Order split, reads as Frostpunk to anyone in the city-builder/idle audience. 'Don't wake the Sleeper' is the Lovecraft taboo every reader expects.
proposed_turn: Rename the role away from 'faith-keeper'; give the folk faith a taboo that fits the Tally instead of 'don't wake it', for instance 'never thank the warmth' (it keeps accounts), so the faith's partial truth is about debt, which the Hearth's cost later pays.

id: B24 / B25 / B28 (the map marks your camp; the ward opens only for you; keepers step politely around you)
resembles: Horizon Zero Dawn (doors and machines that recognise Aloy alone)
the chosen-one door generally
why: Three 'the old machine knows only you' beats in a row signal chosen one, a trope writing-craft.md §4 puts on the worn list, and the plan's later point is that you are not special. 'Step politely around you' is a nice detail, keep it.
proposed_turn: Let the ward open for N3 as well (also a holder) and not for you on a second try, which undercuts specialness and becomes a Q3 clue; or have the keepers' politeness be a filing behaviour (they log you, they don't spare you).

id: B29 / B31 / B39 / B44 / cast.md N6 Hale (old mentor with a secret; confession not betrayal; proposes the proven way)
resembles: Star Wars (Obi-Wan's withheld truth)
Dumbledore (the mentor who arranged the sacrifice)
Final Fantasy X (Auron, and the summoners' 'proven way')
why: world.md keeps this trope 'as promised' on purpose, which is legitimate. The turn already in it (he signed your papers and lives on a ledger of his own years, 'a little of what the Unpaid became') is good, but B39 states it as a confession scene and B44 has him explain the plan. Watch the telling.
proposed_turn: Let the confession be a document the player finds in R4 with his signature before he says anything (he notices the player has read it, and B39 is him not denying it), so the player completes it and the scene is the silence.

id: B34 / cast.md N9 Ilse (an old woman you looked after when she was eight; you haven't aged)
resembles: Frieren: Beyond Journey's End (the unageing one meeting grown-up children they once cared for)
Doctor Who, 'The Girl in the Fireplace'
Highlander / Interview with the Vampire
why: The unageing protagonist recognised by an aged child is a staple; Frieren made it the genre's best-known version recently. 'She asks if you remember her. You don't.' is the stock sad exchange. H4's decades-old snare tied your way is the better clue and is shipped.
proposed_turn: Let N9 recognise the snare knot before she recognises you, and not be sure it is you (she thinks you're your own son, and you can't correct her); the player completes it from the snares.

id: B40 Concord mirror (a mirror in the registry hall shows your real age)
resembles: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray
Harry Potter (the Mirror of Erised)
Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (age catching up)
why: The truth-showing mirror is one of the oldest props in fantasy, and B40 already carries the registry reveal; the mirror spells out what B34 (N9) already showed.
proposed_turn: Cut it, and let the registry entry's date of binding do the arithmetic for the player.

id: B38 / creatures.md Hollowed clerk, the Unpaid (clerks still filing in a dead city; liches killed by breaking their anchors)
resembles: Dark Souls (Hollows repeating their last task)
Ray Bradbury, 'There Will Come Soft Rains'
D&D (lich and phylactery)
Harry Potter (horcruxes)
why: world.md says liches 'are liches and die by their anchor' on purpose, and the anchors being tally-sticks and ledgers is a turn in object. Hollowed clerks still at their desks are Dark Souls hollows plus Bradbury. 'Some can be walked home; they never recover' is good pathos.
proposed_turn: Keep the lich convention, but make breaking an anchor cost the town something it wanted: an Unpaid's ledger is also the only copy of a record (a name list, a debt the Warm are owed), so killing it destroys evidence.

id: B46 / B47 / world.md 'The dead god, implied' (ribs as ridges, wrong-shaped dunes, it breathes, a scream from far down)
resembles: Xenoblade Chronicles (a world on the corpses of titans)
Norse Ymir (a world made from a giant's body)
N. K. Jemisin, The Broken Earth (a living, wronged Earth)
Tolkien, Moria's drums in the deep / the Balrog (the sound from far below)
Scavengers Reign / Made in Abyss (unsure)
why: The land as a giant body with ribs for ridges is the most common form of the implied dead god; a reader sees 'long curved ridges at regular intervals' and says 'ribs' at once, so the implication is a reveal. The Godsgrave guardrail bans the corpse-shaped map but ribs are a corpse-shaped landscape. The cooling and breathing are subtler and enough.
proposed_turn: Drop the ribs and the scream; keep cooling and breathing, and let the uncanny be in the Tally: exchanges with it don't balance, which the journal records as figures. A god implied by bad arithmetic fits this world and nobody has filed it.

id: creatures.md Leaners / the dune thing / the stilled
resembles: Annihilation (unsure)
SCP Foundation's negative-space register
why: Unexplained figures leaning at a falling angle who turn their faces away, a dune that moves, animals stilled mid-step that turn their heads in the Clear: restrained, wrong behaviour over wrong looks (creature-design.md §2 rule 2), kept few and unexplained at one depth. The 'blank sketch page with one line' is very good. Keep.

id: creatures.md Greycoats, Tallymen, Mourners (the Taking: animals that ate the dead took one human trait)
resembles: creature-design.md's Annihilation reference for 'familiar with one wrong detail'
why: Wolves that sit facing the fire waiting to be asked in, crows that count the town in Concord numbers and drop the count before a death is told, cats that learned latches 'the way we did: by having hands'. One premise, one behavioural change each, pathos over disgust. This is the best material in the plan and a reader would not file it as template. Keep.

id: creatures.md Ledger-hound (brass-and-bone dog that tracked runaway holders, sits at your feet)
resembles: Fahrenheit 451's Mechanical Hound (unsure as an echo)
why: A hunting construct that finds the holder and guards them, fighting anyone beside them, is a clue told through behaviour and fits the 'made things' rule. Fine.

id: B42 (the Breaking's record: the first keel failed because its holder refused; it is N3)
resembles: Omelas (the one who walks away)
why: 'The refusal was right and broke the world anyway', with the refuser being the gentlest person in town, is a real turn on the gentle-stranger trope, and 'never stated; laid side by side' is the right telling. Its weakness is the clueing (see N3), not the beat.

id: B49 (your torn front pages at the refuser's keel: a previous you got this far, with a half-drawn design of a keel held by many)
resembles: Returnal / Edge of Tomorrow / Outer Wilds (the past self or past civilisation that left the solution)
Planescape: Torment
why: The past self hands you the answer, which is a tidy convenience: the solution arrives as a found blueprint rather than from the town. The plan says the theme is 'the nobody and the town achieve it together', and B49 gives the idea to a previous you. 'You had the idea before; you didn't have a town' is a line explaining its own meaning (llm-tells #11).
proposed_turn: Let the pages hold the list of names and a design that failed (one previous you tried a shared keel with too few people and it is why there are layers), so the town's version is built against a known failure, not from a blueprint.

id: B52 / E-a ('people find what they've given: a song's second verse, the colour of a door back home. They mostly shrug. Some don't.')
resembles: Kazuo Ishiguro, The Buried Giant (shared forgetting as the price of peace)
the 'everyone gives a little' ending of many community-power finales
why: The cost is softened to charm: second verses and door colours. llm-writing.md lists softened dark registers and tidy endings as the measured fiction tells, and flat-story.md warns of upward drift in a grim story. 'Nobody forgets everything' is a guarantee the story hasn't earned.
proposed_turn: Let one cost bite and be named by object: someone forgets a dead child's face, or the town's spoken names of the dead (S-names) are what the Hearth spends first, so what is given is the grief itself. Keep 'they mostly shrug' after it.

id: B53 (the morning after: roofs clean; someone sweeps them anyway out of habit; a lot of work to do)
why: Understated, concrete, no maxim, no fanfare, play continues; the sweeping is a turn the reader completes (the habit of the ash outlives the ash). It risks being one grace note too neat, but it is earned if B52 bites.

id: E-b (you alone, rebound; you'll forget again; the stool goes in the cellar for next time; 'You said yes. Of course you did.')
resembles: Dark Souls (Link the Fire)
Hollow Knight (the Hollow Knight ending: take the vessel's place)
why: The quiet sad ending is fine (the owner said yes to it), but it closes on two loop-closers at once: the stool placed for next time and the catchphrase. The catchphrase as last line is the aphoristic close llm-tells.md rules out; the stool placed is a tidy bow.
proposed_turn: End on one concrete act and stop: you cut the stool's leg short. No line.

id: regions.md R5 'red glow on the horizon that is never reached'; mysteries 'what lies past the glow' kept for expansions
resembles: The Road / The Dog Stars (the destination never reached)
why: writing-craft.md §4 lists 'the journey with no destination' as usable with a turn; here the turn is that the story's goal shrinks to keeping one valley, so the unreached glow is the point, not a stall. Fine.

id: cast.md arrival tiers named survival / safety / belonging / esteem / self-actualization
resembles: Maslow's hierarchy of needs (textbook)
why: If these tier names are ever player-facing (spine B10 'Safety tier', B33 'Self-actualization tier'), a reader sees a psychology diagram, which is the 'template' read the reviewer gave. As internal scaffolding it is fine. Unsure whether they ship.
proposed_turn: Keep the ladder internally; in player text name each tier by what draws people (fire, wall, table, forge, books).

id: cast.md N1 Tamsin arc ('late she offers you a job and visibly hopes you'll decline; she says nothing about it')
why: The first follower who stays is a convention kept on purpose; the late turn (the one who hands you offers hopes you'll refuse, and doesn't say so) is implied and dry. Keep.

id: cast.md N7 smith never fixing the stool; N4 'says the words' then doesn't at B47
why: Small recurring behaviours paid by an absence (N4 not saying the words at the scream) are the plan at its best: the change is shown by a missing act. Keep.

id: spine B32 / B44 / world.md telling ('The goal changes from fix the world to keep this part of it, and you said yes to that too'; 'You had the idea before; you didn't have a town'; E-a 'the least important you've been all game and the most free')
why: Explanation where the plan should leave the step to the player: these lines state the theme the beat shows. As design notes they're fine; the risk is that they leak verbatim into game text, as llm-writing.md and llm-tells #11 warn. 'The most free' is a moral.
proposed_turn: Mark these as design intent only in the beat notes, and write the player-facing lines as the concrete act each beat contains, ending before the meaning.
